verdicts.notes: Two searches. Gawrilow & Gollwitzer (2008), Cognitive Therapy and Research 32, 261-280, exists with this title (Springer lists it as '...in Children with ADHD'; the Konstanz lab page as '...in ADHD children'). Search summaries confirm two experiments in which children with ADHD were randomly assigned to a goal-intention condition or an if-then-plan condition on a computer Go/NoGo task; in Study 1 the if-then planners improved inhibition to the level of children without ADHD, and Study 2 found if-then plans plus stimulant medication gave the highest suppression. Not seen: per-study sample sizes, and the Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006 backdrop figure (d about 0.65, 94 tests) was not searched. Note that only Study 1 is the 'to the level of non-ADHD children' result; Study 2 was a medication-combination design, so the claim's plural 'studies' slightly stretches it.
verdicts.corrected_source: Gawrilow, C., & Gollwitzer, P. M. (2008). Implementation intentions facilitate response inhibition in children with ADHD. Cognitive Therapy and Research, 32(2), 261-280.
verdicts.corrected_numbers: Two randomised laboratory experiments; Study 1: if-then plan group matched non-ADHD comparison children on Go/NoGo inhibition; Study 2: if-then plans + stimulant medication gave the best inhibition. Sample sizes not shown in search summaries. A 2025 British Journal of Psychology meta-analysis (Breitwieser et al., 'The effectiveness of implementation intentions in children') appeared in results and would be the better general-population backdrop than Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006.

verdicts.notes: Two searches. Gawrilow, Gollwitzer & Oettingen (2011), Cognitive Therapy and Research 35, 442-455, exists with this exact title. Summaries confirm Study 1 (45 inpatient children with ADHD, mean age 10.7) increased delay-of-gratification performance after forming implementation intentions, and Study 2 replicated this in 47 outpatient children with ADHD (mean age 10.3) and 40 children without ADHD (mean age 11.3). The companion paper 'If-then plans benefit executive functions in children with ADHD' (Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology 30(6), 616-646, 2011) also exists and reports fewer perseveration errors on a modified WCST shifting task, with ADHD children performing as well as non-ADHD children. Random assignment is not stated verbatim in the 2011 summaries (it is for the 2008 paper), and the implication's 'single concrete plan, not a list' was not visible.
verdicts.corrected_source: Gawrilow, C., Gollwitzer, P. M., & Oettingen, G. (2011). If-then plans benefit delay of gratification performance in children with and without ADHD. Cognitive Therapy and Research, 35(5), 442-455. Companion: same authors (2011), If-then plans benefit executive functions in children with ADHD, Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 30(6), 616-646.
verdicts.corrected_numbers: Study 1 n=45 inpatient children with ADHD (mean age 10.7); Study 2 n=47 outpatient children with ADHD (mean age 10.3) plus n=40 without ADHD (mean age 11.3). Task-switching paper: fewer perseveration errors on a modified WCST; ADHD-vs-non-ADHD gap removed. Companion paper PDF: https://www.psy.uni-hamburg.de/arbeitsbereiche/paedagogische-psychologie-und-motivation/personen/oettingen-gabriele/dokumente/gawrilow-gollwitzer-oettingen-2011-executive-functions.pdf

verdicts.notes: Two searches. Reid, Trout & Schartz (2005), Exceptional Children 71(4), 361-377, exists and is a meta-analysis of four self-regulation interventions for children with ADHD (self-monitoring, self-monitoring plus reinforcement, self-management, self-reinforcement), with combined effect sizes greater than 1.0 for on-task behaviour, inappropriate behaviour, and academic accuracy and productivity. What the summaries do NOT show is the claim's ranking: nothing seen says self-monitoring alone is 'the largest and most consistent' tool; the >1.0 figure is pooled across all four intervention types. The count of 16 studies and the single-subject design of the included studies were not visible in any summary, so 'almost all single-subject designs' remains unverified (a 2019 Harrison et al. single-case review of ADHD classroom interventions appeared in results and would be a better source for that point).
verdicts.corrected_source: Reid, R., Trout, A. L., & Schartz, M. (2005). Self-regulation interventions for children with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Exceptional Children, 71(4), 361-377.
verdicts.corrected_numbers: Combined effect sizes > 1.0 across the four self-regulation intervention types for on-task behaviour, inappropriate behaviour, and academic accuracy and productivity. Number of studies and per-intervention breakdown not shown; the claim should say 'self-regulation interventions including self-monitoring', not that self-monitoring is the largest.

verdicts.notes: Two searches. Fabiano et al. (2010), School Psychology Review 39(2), 219-239, exists with this title and 12 listed authors. Summaries confirm a randomised design: 33 children with ADHD in special-education placements assigned to a consultant-supported DRC built from IEP goals versus 30 in business-as-usual (63 total), with positive effects on observed classroom functioning, IEP goal attainment, and teacher-rated academic productivity and disruptive behaviour, and more DRC children normalised on disruptive behaviour and impairment. The home-consequence link is confirmed: parents of DRC children took classes teaching them to provide home rewards for the card. Not seen: the 'three to five targets, daily pass criterion, reviewed the same day' structure (generic DRC description, not visible in summaries) and the trial length ('school year'). A new 2025 RCT of the same IEP-plus-DRC design (PubMed 40587316) appeared in results and reported about 4.5 fewer rule violations per 30-minute class.
verdicts.corrected_source: Fabiano, G. A., Vujnovic, R. K., Pelham, W. E., Waschbusch, D. A., Massetti, G. M., Pariseau, M. E., Naylor, J., Yu, J., Robins, M., Carnefix, T., Greiner, A. R., & Volker, M. (2010). Enhancing the effectiveness of special education programming for children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder using a daily report card. School Psychology Review, 39(2), 219-239.
verdicts.corrected_numbers: n=63 (33 DRC, 30 control), randomised; outcomes: classroom observations, IEP goal attainment, teacher-rated academic productivity and disruptive behaviour; parents trained to give home rewards. Effect sizes not shown. Replication: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40587316/

verdicts.notes: Two searches. Langberg, Epstein, Becker, Girio-Herrera & Vaughn (2012), School Psychology Review 41(3), 342-364, exists: 47 middle-school students with ADHD (grades 6-8) randomised to HOPS or waitlist, delivered by 17 school mental health providers in five districts; significant parent-rated gains in organised action, materials management, planning and homework completion, with no significant teacher-rated improvement. The 2018 scale-up also checks out: Langberg et al., Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 86(1), 39-55, 280 students randomised to HOPS, CHIEF or waitlist, up to 16 sessions over 11 weeks, both interventions improving parent-rated homework problems. Not seen anywhere: the effect magnitude ('large', d about 1), the 3-month follow-up, the 'two parent meetings' and 'weekly parent check' components, and the 2018 claim that HOPS beat CHIEF on planning and organisation. The direction is right; the size and the parent-check detail are unverified.
verdicts.corrected_source: Langberg, J. M., Epstein, J. N., Becker, S. P., Girio-Herrera, E., & Vaughn, A. J. (2012). Evaluation of the Homework, Organization, and Planning Skills (HOPS) intervention for middle school students with ADHD as implemented by school mental health providers. School Psychology Review, 41(3), 342-364. Scale-up: Langberg et al. (2018). Overcoming the research-to-practice gap: A randomized trial with two brief homework and organization interventions for students with ADHD as implemented by school mental health providers. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 86(1), 39-55.
verdicts.corrected_numbers: 2012: n=47, grades 6-8, HOPS vs waitlist; parent-rated gains significant, teacher-rated not significant; effect sizes not shown. 2018: n=280, HOPS vs CHIEF vs waitlist, up to 16 sessions in 11 weeks; both improved parent-rated homework problems; HOPS-over-CHIEF difference not shown. 2018 paper: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29172596/

verdicts.notes: Two searches. Bikic, Reichow, McCauley, Ibrahim & Sukhodolsky (2017), Clinical Psychology Review 52, 108-123, exists and is a meta-analysis of 12 RCTs (1,054 children: 576 treatment, 478 control). Effect sizes seen: organisational skills g=0.54 teacher-rated, g=0.83 parent-rated; inattention g=0.26 teacher-rated, g=0.56 parent-rated; academic performance g=0.33 teacher-rated and g=0.29 for GPA. The claim's recalled numbers are close for teacher ratings, organisation and academics, but the claim's wording is wrong in two places: parent-rated organisation is 'large' (0.83), not 'moderate', and parent-rated inattention is moderate (0.56), not 'only small'. The practical conclusion (planning tools move organisation more than grades) still holds.
verdicts.corrected_source: Bikic, A., Reichow, B., McCauley, S. A., Ibrahim, K., & Sukhodolsky, D. G. (2017). Meta-analysis of organizational skills interventions for children and adolescents with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Clinical Psychology Review, 52, 108-123.
verdicts.corrected_numbers: 12 RCTs, n=1,054. Organisational skills: teacher g=0.54 (95% CI 0.17-0.91), parent g=0.83 (0.32-1.34). Inattention: teacher g=0.26 (0.01-0.52), parent g=0.56 (0.38-0.74). Academic performance: teacher-rated g=0.33 (0.14-0.51), GPA g=0.29 (0.07-0.51).

verdicts.notes: Two searches. Evans, Owens, Wymbs & Ray (2018), Journal of Clinical Child & Adolescent Psychology 47(2), 157-198, exists and is a systematic review of 2012-2016 literature using modified Division 12 criteria, updating Evans, Owens & Bunford (2014). Summaries confirm the first half of the claim and the recalled classifications: behavioural parent training, behavioural classroom management, behavioural peer interventions (omitted by the claim) and their combination are well-established; organisation training is well-established; the combined training intervention is Level 2 probably efficacious; neurofeedback Level 3 possibly efficacious; cognitive training Level 4 experimental. The second half of the claim (visual timers, checklists alone, dashboards and weekly-review rituals 'have no independent ADHD evidence base') is not something the review says; it is the agent's inference from those tools not appearing as rated treatments, and the review's inclusion of the daily report card under behavioural classroom management was not visible in summaries. Present it as inference, not as a finding of the review.
verdicts.corrected_source: Evans, S. W., Owens, J. S., Wymbs, B. T., & Ray, A. R. (2018). Evidence-based psychosocial treatments for children and adolescents with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Journal of Clinical Child & Adolescent Psychology, 47(2), 157-198.
verdicts.corrected_numbers: Well-established: BPT, BCM, BPI, their combination, and organisation training. Probably efficacious (Level 2): combined training intervention with academic and social components. Possibly efficacious (Level 3): neurofeedback. Experimental (Level 4): cognitive training. No rating exists for timers, checklists, dashboards or weekly reviews as stand-alone treatments.
